intro.html: Some things turn up wherever you look. These words describe how widely something is found (ubiquitous, prevalent, universal), how it spreads (pervasive, rampant, permeate, saturate, diffuse), which kind wins out (predominant) and something that belongs to one place (endemic).

Found everywhere: ubiquitous, universal. Common: prevalent; predominant (the most common or strongest). Spreading through: pervasive, permeate, saturate (to the very full), diffuse (spread out) and rampant (out of control). Always found in one place: endemic.

words.def: found everywhere; seeming to be everywhere at once
words.ex: Phones are so {ubiquitous} now that it is hard to find a bus rider without one.
words.ctx: Twenty years ago only a few cafés offered free internet, but today it is {ubiquitous}: libraries, buses, parks and even some campgrounds have it.

mn.cue: YOU BIKE WITH US: bikes everywhere
mn.text: In this town, everyone calls out “You bike with us!” Bikes are on every path, every rack and every porch: they are {ubiquitous}.

scene.alt: Bicycles fill every corner of a park while two friends in helmets wave.

words.def: spreading through every part of something
words.ex: The {pervasive} smell of popcorn drifted through every corner of the theater.
words.ctx: Worry about the coming storm was {pervasive}; it showed in the empty store shelves, the boarded-up windows and the anxious faces on every street.
words.etym: From Latin pervadere, “to go through”: per (through) + vadere (to go).

mn.cue: per-VASE-ive: VASES all THROUGH the house
mn.text: Granny Mae loves flowers so much that there are vases on every table, shelf and windowsill in her house. Flowers are {pervasive} there.

scene.alt: A grandmother holds a bouquet in a room crowded with flower vases on every surface.

words.def: widespread; common in a place or at a time
words.ex: Colds are most {prevalent} in the winter months.
words.ctx: Hats were once {prevalent}, so common that hardly anyone left home without one, but by the 1970s most people went out bareheaded.
words.etym: From Latin praevalere, “to be stronger, to win out”: prae (before, above) + valere (to be strong).

mn.text: When it rains in our town, nearly all of us carry red umbrellas. Red umbrellas are {prevalent} here.

scene.alt: On a rainy city street, nearly everyone carries the same red umbrella.

words.def: spreading or growing out of control
words.ex: Weeds grew {rampant} in the empty lot behind the school.
words.ctx: Before the new rules, cheating in the online game had been {rampant}; nearly every top score on the board turned out to be fake.
words.etym: From Old French rampant, “climbing, rearing up,” from ramper, “to climb.” In old coats of arms, a lion rampant rears up on its hind legs.

mn.text: One ram jumps the fence, then ten more follow. Soon rams are running wild all over the farm: they are {rampant}!

scene.alt: A flock of rams leaps and runs wild across a farm while a grandfather shouts for them to stop.

words.def: most common, strongest or most important
words.ex: Blue is the {predominant} color in Kai’s room: blue walls, a blue rug and a blue bedspread.
words.ctx: Many languages are spoken in the city, but English is {predominant}; it appears on nearly every sign and is taught in nearly every school.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin praedominari, “to rule over”: prae (before, above) + dominari (to rule).

mn.text: In Zoe’s garden, nearly every flower is yellow; only one is red. Yellow is the {predominant} color.

scene.alt: A girl in a yellow dress cheers in a garden of yellow flowers with just one red one.

words.def: true of, used by or including everyone or everything
words.ex: A smile is a {universal} sign of friendliness.
words.ctx: The love of music seems almost {universal}: every culture that has ever been studied has had songs, from lullabies to work chants.
words.etym: From Latin universalis, from universus, “all together, whole”: unus (one) + versus (turned).

mn.cue: UNIVERSE-al: true across the whole UNIVERSE
mn.text: Pip lands on a faraway planet, and the robot there waves hello, just like at home. Waving hello is {universal}!

scene.alt: A boy in a space helmet waves at a robot on another planet, and the robot waves back.

words.def: regularly found in a particular place or among a particular group
words.ex: The kiwi is {endemic} to New Zealand; in the wild, it lives nowhere else on Earth.
words.ctx: Some problems come and go, but traffic jams are {endemic} to the city: they happen every single morning, as steady as the sunrise.
words.etym: From Greek endemos, “native, belonging to a people”: en (in) + demos (people, district).
words.note: Endemic (always present in one place) is not epidemic (a sudden outbreak that spreads widely and then fades).

mn.cue: EN = IN: found IN one place only
mn.text: The purple parrot lives on this one little island and nowhere else in the world. It is {endemic} to the island.

scene.alt: A purple parrot perches on a tiny island beside a sign that says Only Here.

words.def: to spread through every part of something
words.ex: The smell of fresh bread {permeated} the whole house.
words.ctx: Excitement {permeated} the school in the week before the big game; even the cafeteria workers wore team colors, and every hallway rang with cheers.
words.etym: From Latin permeare, “to pass through”: per (through) + meare (to go, to pass).

mn.cue: PER (through) + MEATE: spreads all the way THROUGH
mn.text: Nana Lou bakes bread, and the warm smell drifts through the window, down the street and into every house. It {permeates} the whole village.

scene.alt: A grandmother holds a fresh loaf, and its smell drifts down the street to two neighbors who sniff happily.

words.def: to soak completely; to fill so full that no more can be added
words.ex: The garden hose {saturated} the flower bed until water pooled on top.
words.ctx: The sponge was so {saturated} that it could not hold another drop; every new splash simply ran off onto the counter.
words.etym: From Latin saturare, “to fill full,” from satur, “full.”

mn.cue: SAT-u-RATE: he SAT in it, now SOAKED
mn.text: Sami sat right down in the biggest puddle on the playground, and his pants soaked up every drop they could hold. They are {saturated}!

scene.alt: A boy sits in a huge puddle, soaked through, while a teen laughs.

words.def: to spread out over a wide area
words.ex: A few drops of food coloring {diffused} slowly through the glass of water.
words.ctx: The paper lampshade {diffused} the light, spreading a soft glow across the whole room instead of one harsh, bright spot.
words.etym: From Latin diffundere, “to pour out, to spread”: dis (apart) + fundere (to pour).
words.note: Diffuse (spread out) is not defuse (calm a tense situation). As an adjective, diffuse (dih-FYOOS) means spread out or wordy.

mn.text: Pop! Lila’s pillow bursts, and the feathers spread out over the whole room, every which way. They {diffuse}.

scene.alt: A girl's pillow bursts, and feathers spread out all over her bedroom.

after.html: Two pairs to keep apart. Endemic means always present in one place or group, while an epidemic is a sudden outbreak that spreads widely and then fades. And diffuse (spread out) is not defuse (calm a tense situation): a lamp diffuses light; a friend defuses an argument.

opts.s: In our old neighborhood, red brick houses are {prevalent}; you can count the wooden ones on one hand.
opts.why: Something common and widespread in a place is prevalent.

items.q: True or false: endemic describes something that suddenly spreads fast and then fades away.
items.why: False. That describes an epidemic. Endemic means regularly found in one place or group, at a steady level.

items.q: Open the windows, and the smell of fresh paint will ______ into the yard. Which word fits?
items.why: To diffuse is to spread out. Defuse means to calm a tense situation.

items.q: Universal is built from uni- (one) and vers (turn). Literally, something universal is…
items.why: Latin universus meant turned into one, all together: so universal things include everyone and everything.

items.q: Which word best describes weeds that have spread out of control?
items.why: Rampant means spreading or growing without control.

items.q: Type the word, from Latin ubique (everywhere), that means found everywhere.
items.why: Ubiquitous things seem to be everywhere at once.
